newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi king says pilgrims should avoid politics.
newsitem.headline: Saudi king says pilgrims should avoid politics.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's King Fahd urged the two million Moslems expected to perform this year's haj pilgrimage to holy sites in the kingdom to steer clear of politics, the official Saudi Press Agency reported on Tuesday.
It said the king made his comments at the weekly cabinet meeting in Riyadh on Monday night.

King Fahd said he hoped pilgrims understood that Saudi Arabia -- custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines in Mecca and Medina -- was always eager to perform its duties in such a way as to not cause concern for pilgrims, the agency said.

"Therefore, the kingdom of Saudi Arabia stresses the need for the pilgrimage to be free from any political aims because the kingdom deeply believes that God has made pilgrimage a duty to be performed without obscenity or wantonness," it quoted the king as saying.

Saudi Arabia has over the past two months reiterated warnings that it would deal harshly with any violators of its ban on political activity during haj, which falls in mid-April this year when two million Moslems -- half of them from outside the kingdom -- coverge on Mecca and Medina.

The warnings appear aimed at Iran, which insists on holding political rallies mainly directed against the United States and Israel in defiance of the Saudi ban. Saudi Arabia says haj is a religious duty that should not be politicised.
Iran boycotted haj for three years after some 400 people, mainly Iranian pilgrims, were killed in clashes in 1987 between Saudi police and Iranians holding a political rally in Mecca.
The row over haj usually further strains already tense relations between the two powerful regional oil producers.

Iran has been trying to improve ties with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf Arab states and its desire for better relations has been reflected by a softer tone used by Iranian media and officials towards the kingdom in recent weeks even when calling for rallies during haj.
